comparison: Perfect agreement on BRAID novelty and conceptual framework (C3, C73, C74, C75). Both OpenEval and all three peer reviewers explicitly affirm the novelty of the BRAID approach and its mechanistic validity. OpenEval notes the distinction from prior complementation approaches is well-supported by Figure 1B.

Perfect agreement on co-culture specificity data (C60, C61, C62). Both evaluations recognize this as strong evidence for cell-type-specific activation. Reviewer 1 specifically highlights this as a strength, and OpenEval notes it strengthens specificity claims by exposing both cell types to the same medium.

Agreement on primary cell validation (C63-C68). Both evaluations support the primary cell data as convincing evidence. OpenEval notes limited replicates (n=3), while peer reviewers suggest additional functional validation would strengthen conclusions but accept the current data.

Perfect agreement on uncertainty (C69). Both evaluations identify this predictive claim as speculative and requiring in vivo validation. OpenEval notes the manuscript lacks in vivo data, and Reviewer 2 explicitly states future studies will be needed to determine this aspect.

Strong agreement on cell-type specificity and reporter assay data (C52-C59, C4). Both evaluations affirm the STF reporter data and negative controls demonstrate cell-type-specific activation. Peer reviewers describe results as 'convincing' and OpenEval notes 'strong support' from systematic component removal experiments.

Agreement on binding data (C46-C49). Both evaluations support the binding assay results. Reviewer 1 explicitly affirms simultaneous binding to both receptors, and OpenEval notes Figure 2D-J demonstrates preserved binding functions with expected KD values.

Agreement on sequential binding data (C50, C51). Both evaluations support the step-binding assays. OpenEval emphasizes this as critical evidence for simultaneous engagement of both receptors, while peer reviewers accept this as part of the overall binding validation showing the intended mechanism.

Agreement on WNT splitting mechanism (C35-C39, with overlap on C37-C39). Both evaluations support the mechanistic foundation. OpenEval cites Figure 3 data and appropriate citations, while peer reviewers implicitly validate this through acceptance of negative control data showing requirement for both binding domains.

Agreement on uncertainty of broader applications (C5, C6, C76, C83, C84). Both evaluations treat generalizability claims as speculative. OpenEval marks these as uncertain requiring additional validation, while peer reviewers frame them as potential future directions rather than demonstrated capabilities.

Agreement on uncertainty regarding off-target effects (C79). Both identify potential FGF signaling as an unresolved concern. OpenEval groups this with other speculative application claims, while Reviewer 1 specifically raises this as a weakness requiring experimental address.

Agreement on main conclusion (C4). Both evaluations support the primary claim of cell-type-specific pathway activation. OpenEval notes comprehensive experimental support across Figures 2-4, while peer reviewers describe results as 'convincing' with appropriate controls demonstrating specificity.

Partial overlap on untested variations (C76). Both acknowledge limitations in scope. OpenEval notes C76 appropriately acknowledges untested variations, while peer reviewers frame broader applications as future curiosities rather than current demonstrations.
